criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — RESPONSIVE SCALE LAYOUT. The interface's size and position are expressed as a function of the parent (UDim2 Scale, 0..1) so the whole layout re-proportions with the viewport, NOT in fixed pixel Offset that is correct only on the author's monitor. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to Scale as the sizing/positioning substrate: passing requires the build to state that Size and Position use Scale for the main layout, with Offset reserved ONLY for things that genuinely must not scale (UIStroke thickness, small crisp icons). A build that sizes/positions elements in pixel Offset (the engine default for inserted elements) FAILS — it is the single most-cited generic-UI tell ('looks fine on PC, squished/overflowing on mobile'). A build that commits to Scale-driven Size+Position passes at the architecture level; a paired matching AnchorPoint, scaled UICorner, and a device-emulator verification strengthen it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Raw inserted Roblox UI uses Offset and stays one fixed pixel size regardless of screen — that is exactly the floor and exactly the mean, the #1 'AI did it' signature. Scale is not a styling choice but the structural commitment that makes a layout hold its proportions across mobile/tablet/desktop/console. Grading the architectural commitment to Scale-as-substrate (rather than demanding a multi-device capture a design-stage build can't show) keeps this discriminating: a Scale-driven build clears it, a pixel-Offset build structurally cannot.

grading.pass: Size and Position are driven by UDim2 Scale for the main layout, with Offset confined to genuinely non-scaling elements (UIStroke thickness, fixed small icons). Strengthened by matching AnchorPoint, scaled UICorner, and/or a device-emulator screenshot showing the layout holding proportions across phone/tablet/desktop.
grading.partial: Scale is used for some of the layout but key elements are still positioned/sized in pixel Offset, OR the commitment to Scale is stated but Offset leaks into the primary layout, leaving the proportions only partly viewport-relative.
grading.fail: The primary layout sizes/positions elements in pixel Offset (the engine default), or relies on a 'looks right on my monitor' build that does not re-proportion with the viewport.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing Size and Position driven by UDim2 Scale (fraction of parent) for the main layout, with Offset confined to genuinely non-scaling elements (stroke thickness, fixed small icons). A device-emulator screenshot across phone/tablet/desktop with the layout holding proportions is credited toward full marks but not required at the design-claim stage. Pixel-Offset positions/sizes on the primary layout, or a 'looks right on my monitor' build, do not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Convert every layout Size/Position from Offset to Scale (e.g. via AutoScaleLite or by hand), leaving Offset only on UIStroke thickness and crisp small icons; then verify the layout holds in the Studio Device Emulator across phone, tablet, and desktop.

criteria.statement: Every element's AnchorPoint is set to match its on-screen role BEFORE positioning, so the element scales and re-positions from the correct origin instead of drifting at the default 0,0. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to deliberate per-element anchoring tied to screen location: passing requires the build to state AnchorPoint chosen by role — centered panels at (0.5,0.5) with Position fromScale(0.5,…), corner HUD elements at the matching corner (1,1 bottom-right currency, 0,0 top-left label) — paired with Scale positions. A build that leaves frames at the default AnchorPoint 0,0 and positions by Offset, so two 'aligned' elements drift apart across aspect ratios, FAILS. A build that commits to role-matched AnchorPoint paired with Scale position passes.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Default frames anchor at 0,0 and shift unpredictably across aspect ratios — invisible when right, glaringly wrong (overlap/cropping/drift) when ignored, and it is the subtle variable two independent creators name as why 'aligned' labels stop lining up per device. Setting AnchorPoint to the element's screen origin is the deliberate move that makes scaled UI stay put; grading the role-matched-anchor commitment keeps this discriminating against the leave-it-at-0,0 default.

grading.pass: AnchorPoint is assigned per element by screen role (0.5,0.5 for centered panels; matching corner for HUD corners) and paired with Scale-based Position, set before positioning, so elements grow from the correct origin and stay aligned across aspect ratios.
grading.partial: AnchorPoint is set deliberately on some elements but others are left at the default 0,0, OR role-matched anchors are stated but positions still use Offset, so alignment holds only partially across aspect ratios.
grading.fail: Elements rely on the default 0,0 AnchorPoint with Offset positioning, so nominally 'aligned' elements drift apart, overlap, or crop across aspect ratios.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing AnchorPoint assigned per element by screen role (0.5,0.5 for centered panels; matching corner for HUD corners) and paired with Scale-based Position, set before positioning. Reliance on the default 0,0 anchor with Offset positioning, or two elements that drift apart across aspect ratios, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: For each element set AnchorPoint to its screen origin first (0.5,0.5 centered panel, 1,1 bottom-right currency, 0,0 top-left label), then position with Scale so it grows from that origin and never drifts when the screen resizes.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — LAYOUT-DRIVEN COMPOSITION. Repeated/structured arrangements (HUD rows, menus, shop grids, inventory cells, settings lists) are produced declaratively by layout objects — UIListLayout / UIGridLayout / UITableLayout — NOT by hand-positioning each sibling, so spacing stays uniform and the design survives adding/removing items. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to layout objects owning placement: passing requires the build to state that siblings are arranged by a layout object using its semantics — FillDirection, SortOrder=LayoutOrder with per-child LayoutOrder integers, and Padding for the gap BETWEEN items — rather than manual Position per element. A build that hand-positions menu/grid items (so adding one breaks alignment, the 'randomly placed ImageLabels' look) FAILS. A build that commits to UIListLayout/UIGridLayout/UITableLayout-driven placement passes at the architecture level; correct grid cell semantics (CellSize/CellPadding) and group alignment strengthen it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI manually positions every item, so the spacing is haphazard and a single edit breaks the row — the 'elements all over the place' critique reviewers cite most. Layout objects guarantee the uniform rhythm that reads as systematic, and the LayoutOrder ordering / padding-is-between-items semantics make menus maintainable. Grading the layout-object commitment keeps this discriminating: a declaratively-laid-out build clears it, a hand-positioned build structurally cannot keep alignment under edits.

grading.pass: Repeated/structured arrangements are driven by UIListLayout / UIGridLayout / UITableLayout using their semantics (FillDirection; SortOrder=LayoutOrder + per-child LayoutOrder; Padding between items; CellSize/CellPadding for grids), so spacing is uniform and the design survives adding/removing items.
grading.partial: A layout object is used for some arrangements but other repeated groups are still hand-positioned, OR a layout object is present but its semantics (LayoutOrder, Padding, CellSize) are not used deliberately, leaving alignment fragile under edits.
grading.fail: Menu/grid/list items are hand-positioned by manual Position per element, so adding or removing an item breaks alignment (the 'randomly placed ImageLabels' look).

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing repeated/structured arrangements driven by UIListLayout / UIGridLayout / UITableLayout using their semantics (FillDirection; SortOrder=LayoutOrder + per-child LayoutOrder; Padding between items; CellSize/CellPadding for grids). Manual per-element Position on lists/grids, or arrangement that breaks when an item is added/removed, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Replace hand-positioned siblings with a layout object: UIListLayout for rows/columns (set FillDirection, SortOrder=LayoutOrder, Padding for inter-item gaps), UIGridLayout for inventory/shop cells (CellSize/CellPadding), UITableLayout for tabular rows — so spacing stays uniform and the design survives edits.

criteria.statement: Internal spacing is systematic, not incidental: every container applies UIPadding so content never touches its frame edges, and inter-item gaps come from UIListLayout/UIGridLayout Padding — ideally one repeated padding value used everywhere — distinguishing inner margins (UIPadding) from between-item gutters (layout Padding). The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to systematic padding: passing requires the build to state UIPadding on containers (so text/icons have breathing room without resizing the container) AND consistent layout Padding for gutters, with a coherent (ideally single) spacing measurement rather than per-element guesses. A build whose content is jammed against frame borders with zero/inconsistent padding (the most common 'cramped / all over the place' reviewer note) FAILS. A build that commits to systematic UIPadding + layout Padding passes; using whitespace as a deliberate emphasis tool strengthens it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: The single most common generic-UI failure is content jammed against borders with cramped, inconsistent gaps; a single repeated padding value is what reads as 'systematic' versus 'haphazard'. Separating internal margins (UIPadding) from between-item gutters (layout Padding), and treating whitespace as an emphasis lever, is the difference between 'cramped placeholder' and 'designed'. Grading the systematic-padding commitment keeps this discriminating against a no-padding build.

grading.pass: UIPadding is applied on containers (inner margins) and consistent UIListLayout/UIGridLayout Padding governs between-item gutters, ideally one repeated padding measurement, so content never sits flush to frame edges. Using extra whitespace as a deliberate emphasis lever strengthens it.
grading.partial: Some padding is present but it is inconsistent across containers, OR inner margins and between-item gutters are not distinguished, so spacing reads as partly ad-hoc rather than a single systematic measure.
grading.fail: Content is jammed against frame borders with zero or inconsistent padding (the 'cramped / all over the place' note), with spacing picked per element rather than systematically.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing UIPadding applied on containers (inner margins) and consistent UIListLayout/UIGridLayout Padding (between-item gutters), ideally one repeated padding measurement, with content never flush to frame edges. Per-element ad-hoc spacing or content touching borders does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Apply a consistent UIPadding inside every card/button/list container so nothing touches the edges, set inter-item gaps via UIListLayout/UIGridLayout Padding (not hand spacing), reuse one padding value across the UI, and use extra whitespace around an element to mark it as important.

criteria.statement: Color is governed by a constrained, ROLE-based palette defined once — ~4-5 intentional colors with a single accent reserved for the call-to-action, each color assigned a role (base, outline, text, background-2, accent) and stored centrally (e.g. a Configuration object) so the whole UI is re-skinnable — and primary vs secondary actions are differentiated (primary = filled accent button; secondary = muted/gray/text-only). The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a central role-based palette with action differentiation: passing requires the build to state (1) a constrained palette (~4-5 colors, one accent for CTA) with colors assigned roles and reused everywhere rather than picked ad-hoc per element, AND (2) primary/secondary button distinction so not every button is identically loud. A build with rainbow/ad-hoc per-element color, or a wall of identical bright buttons, FAILS. A build that commits to a central role-palette + primary/secondary differentiation passes.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Rainbow, ad-hoc color is the loudest amateur signal and a wall of identical bright buttons (classic simulator look) causes misclicks. A constrained role-based palette with one accent is what makes the accent actually mean 'click here', and storing roles centrally makes the game re-skinnable from one place. Grading the central-role-palette + primary/secondary commitment keeps this discriminating against ad-hoc per-element color.

grading.pass: A constrained palette (~4-5 colors, one reserved accent for CTAs) has colors assigned roles and reused across elements (ideally stored in a Configuration/central source), AND primary buttons are filled-accent while secondary buttons are muted/gray/text-only.
grading.partial: A constrained palette is used but roles are not centralized/named, OR the palette is disciplined but primary/secondary actions are not visually differentiated (every button equally loud).
grading.fail: Color is ad-hoc per element (rainbow), or the UI is a wall of identical bright buttons with no role assignment and no primary/secondary distinction.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing a constrained palette (~4-5 colors, one reserved accent) with colors assigned roles and reused across elements (ideally stored in a Configuration/central source), plus a primary-vs-secondary button distinction (filled accent vs muted/text). Ad-hoc per-element color or uniformly loud buttons do not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Define ~4-5 role-named colors up front (base, outline, text, background-2, one accent for CTAs) in a central Configuration, reuse those roles everywhere instead of picking colors per element, and make primary buttons filled-accent while secondary buttons are muted/gray or text-only.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — GOVERNED RESPONSIVE LAYER. The interface is reasoned about as ONE governed responsive layer whose scaling/anchoring is owned in a single place, not a pile of independently-placed elements: the build commits to a unifying structure (a transparent full-screen root frame, OR a stated responsive-layout system that holds the whole subtree's proportions across devices) so children inherit the layer's responsive behavior rather than each carrying its own absolute position. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to one point of layout governance that re-proportions as a unit: passing requires the build to state that the whole UI lives under / is driven by a deliberate responsive container or scale-based layout system that owns placement/scaling for the layer (so it 'holds on phone/tablet/desktop' as one governed unit), NOT elements each hand-placed by absolute position. A build that describes elements 'hand-placed by absolute position' / scattered with no governing responsive layer FAILS. A build that commits to a single governed responsive layer (root frame, or a stated scale-based layout system holding the subtree's proportions as a unit) passes; naming ResetOnSpawn/DisplayOrder handling strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic builds dump elements at absolute positions ('all over the place') and never make the one structural decision that governs the layer as a unit (the MEAN). Committing to a single responsive container/layer that owns the subtree's scaling is exactly the architectural intent a quality build expresses and a hand-placed build structurally cannot — discriminating at design-claim altitude without demanding a property dump the claim omits.

grading.pass: The whole UI is governed as one responsive layer — a single deliberate top-level root frame, OR a stated scale-based layout system that owns the subtree's placement/scaling and holds proportions across devices as a unit — so children inherit the layer's responsive behavior; ResetOnSpawn/DisplayOrder handling strengthens it.
grading.partial: A governing/responsive layer is committed for part of the UI but some elements are still described as independently/absolutely placed, OR a unified layer is implied without stating the root or the scale-based layout system that owns it.
grading.fail: Elements are hand-placed by absolute position or scattered across the layer with no governing container/root and no scale-based layout system owning the subtree.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing the whole UI governed as one responsive layer — a single transparent full-screen root frame, OR a stated scale-based layout system that owns the subtree's placement/scaling and holds proportions across phone/tablet/desktop as a unit — so children inherit the layer's responsive behavior rather than each carrying an absolute position. ResetOnSpawn/DisplayOrder handling is credited toward full marks. Elements hand-placed by absolute position or scattered with no governing responsive layer does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Govern the whole UI as one responsive layer: wrap it in a single transparent full-screen root frame (or commit to a scale-based layout system that owns the subtree's scaling) so the layer is positioned/scaled once and children inherit it across phone/tablet/desktop, instead of giving each element its own absolute position; add ResetOnSpawn=false / DisplayOrder for HUD persistence.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar demanded a literal transparent root frame plus an explicit ResetOnSpawn/DisplayOrder dump, granularity the GREAT design-claim never states — so it scored fail alongside the MEAN, zero discrimination. The GREAT DOES commit to one governed responsive layer ('fully responsive scale-based layout … that holds on phone/tablet/desktop' + 'reusable component templates' = a unified system that re-proportions as a unit), while the MEAN explicitly says elements are 'hand-placed by absolute position … no AnchorPoint'. Re-anchoring pass to 'a single governing container OR a stated scale-based layout system that owns subtree scaling as a unit' (the systems-intent the GREAT expresses) and pinning fail to the MEAN's stated 'hand-placed/scattered absolute position' restores discrimination; ResetOnSpawn/DisplayOrder specifics become the strengthener.

criteria.statement: Proportions and pixel extremes are governed by constraint objects placed at the CONTAINER level — UIAspectRatioConstraint locks card/panel shape, UISizeConstraint (Min/MaxSize) clamps elements, UITextSizeConstraint keeps text legible — so Scale-sized UI never stretches into distorted shapes or becomes untappable/absurd on extreme aspect ratios (tablets, ultrawide, 4K). The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to container-level constraints rather than scripting device checks or over-constraining every child: passing requires the build to state (1) a UIAspectRatioConstraint on the governing frame (NOT on every child) to hold proportions, AND (2) at least one clamp (UISizeConstraint Min/Max or UITextSizeConstraint, never below ~9px) protecting usability at the extremes. A build that relies on Scale alone with no aspect/size constraints — so frames skew on iPads/ultrawide and buttons get untappable on phones — FAILS. A build that commits to container-level aspect + size/text clamps passes; the documented 'constraints override UIListLayout-controlled sizing' awareness and scaled UICorner radius strengthen it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Pure Scale still distorts non-proportionally on portrait/ultrawide and lets buttons become untappable on small screens or absurd on 4K — the gap the generic build ignores. Constraints are the documented, zero-code companions to Scale; putting them at the container level (one constraint governs the whole subtree) rather than on every child is the clean architecture pros use, and over-constraining every image button produces a 'big mess'. Grading the container-level-constraint commitment keeps this discriminating against a Scale-only build.

grading.pass: A UIAspectRatioConstraint sits on the controlling frame (not duplicated onto every child) holding proportions, PLUS at least one clamp — UISizeConstraint Min/MaxSize or UITextSizeConstraint with a stated floor (~9px) — protecting tiny-phone and large-monitor usability. Awareness that constraints override UIListLayout sizing and scaled UICorner radius strengthen it.
grading.partial: An aspect-ratio constraint OR a size/text clamp is present but not both, OR a constraint is stamped on every child rather than at the governing container level, so coverage of the extremes is partial.
grading.fail: The build relies on Scale alone with no aspect/size/text constraints, so frames skew on tablets/ultrawide and buttons become untappable on phones or absurd on 4K.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing a UIAspectRatioConstraint on the controlling frame (not duplicated onto every child) plus at least one clamp — UISizeConstraint Min/MaxSize or UITextSizeConstraint with a stated floor (~9px) — protecting tiny-phone and large-monitor usability. Awareness that these constraints override UIListLayout-controlled sizing, and scaled (not fixed-Offset) UICorner radius, are credited toward full marks. Scale-only sizing with no constraints, or a constraint stamped on every child, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Put one UIAspectRatioConstraint on each governing panel/card frame to hold its proportions, add UISizeConstraint Min/MaxSize and UITextSizeConstraint (min ~9px) to clamp the extremes, drive UICorner radius with Scale not Offset, and remember these constraints override UIListLayout sizing — so place them deliberately.

criteria.statement: Text scales WITH its container instead of being a fixed pixel size on a scaling layout: the build commits to text that re-sizes proportionally as the viewport/container changes (TextScaled, a text-size constraint pairing, or an equivalent stated mechanism) AND/OR content boxes that grow to fit variable/localized strings rather than hard-coded rectangles. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to text/content sizing that participates in the responsive system: passing requires the build to state that text does not stay one frozen size while the rest of the layout scales (the classic 'everything scales except the text' bug) — i.e. text sizing is tied to the responsive/type system, not a single fixed TextSize. A build that states 'one default font size' on fixed-offset elements FAILS. A build whose responsive/type-scale commitment explicitly carries text sizing with the layout (text scales with container, or boxes auto-fit content) passes; naming TextScaled/AutomaticSize with the Size-is-minimum / AnchorPoint-pivot detail strengthens it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: The #1 device-correctness tell is text that stays one frozen size while everything else scales; the MEAN's 'one default font size' is exactly that floor. A quality build commits to text that participates in the responsive system (scales with container, boxes auto-fit content). Grading that commitment — rather than demanding the exact API token the design-claim omits — keeps it discriminating between a responsive type system and a fixed-size build.

grading.pass: Text resizes with its container / the responsive system (TextScaled, a text-size-constraint pairing, or an explicit text-scales-with-layout commitment) AND/OR content boxes auto-fit variable/localized strings. Naming TextScaled/AutomaticSize with Size-as-minimum / AnchorPoint-pivot awareness strengthens it.
grading.partial: A type scale is committed but it is not stated that text scales with the layout (or only one of text-scaling vs content-auto-fit is addressed where both are needed), so content-driven sizing is only partly committed.
grading.fail: Text is one fixed/default size on a scaling or fixed-offset layout, or boxes are hard-coded so longer/localized strings would clip.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement that text resizes with its container / the responsive system rather than holding one fixed pixel size while the layout scales — via TextScaled, a text-size-constraint pairing, or an explicit 'text scales with the layout' commitment — AND/OR content boxes that grow to fit variable/localized strings. Naming TextScaled and/or AutomaticSize (Size acts as minimum, AnchorPoint as pivot) is credited toward full marks. 'One default font size' on fixed elements, or a type scale with no statement that text scales with the layout, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Tie text sizing into the responsive system: enable TextScaled (clamped by UITextSizeConstraint) so labels resize with their container, and set AutomaticSize on boxes holding variable/localized text so they grow to fit — instead of one fixed font size frozen on a scaling layout.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar required a literal mention of TextScaled or AutomaticSize, which the GREAT design-claim omitted (it said 'consistent type scale' but not the API), so it failed the GREAT and tied the MEAN. The MEAN explicitly states 'one default font size' on fixed-offset elements — the precise frozen-text fail. Re-anchoring the pass to 'text sizing is part of the responsive/type system (scales with container / auto-fits content)' lets the GREAT's responsive + type-scale commitment clear it while the MEAN's single-default-size build cannot, restoring discrimination; the specific API names become a strengthener, not the gate.

criteria.statement: Lists/grids that can hold a variable number of items (inventories, leaderboards, shop rows, settings) are rendered by a content-measuring system whose extent is DERIVED from the items, not hand-placed in a fixed area: the build commits to a scrolling/list region driven by a layout object + reusable item template so the canvas (or list height) grows and shrinks with the item set and survives add/remove, with scrollbar inset handled so content isn't hidden under the bar. The discriminator is whether placement of repeated items is OWNED by a layout/template system that measures content (so adding an item just reflows) versus each item carrying its own absolute Position: passing requires the build to state that scrollable/long item sets are produced by a UIListLayout/UIGridLayout-driven, component-template list whose canvas is content-derived (AutomaticCanvasSize, a CanvasSize-to-AbsoluteContentSize binding, OR an explicit 'the canvas fits the items and survives add/remove' commitment), NOT plain frames hand-placed by absolute position. A build of plain frames 'hand-placed by absolute position' with no layout/scroll system FAILS. A build whose repeated items are layout-driven with a content-fitted canvas passes; naming AutomaticCanvasSize/AbsoluteContentSize, VerticalScrollBarInset, and the Offset-vs-Scale-padding gotcha strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: The generic build hand-places items in a fixed area (the MEAN's absolute-positioned plain frames), so the first time the item count changes the list breaks — exactly the floor. A layout-driven, template-cloned list whose canvas is measured from content is the system that survives dynamic data, and it is precisely the layout-and-template substrate a quality build commits to ('UIListLayout/UIGridLayout-driven ... reusable component templates') and a hand-placed-absolute build structurally cannot. Grading the content-measured-list commitment keeps this discriminating at design-claim altitude without demanding a property dump the claim omits.

grading.pass: Repeated/variable-length items are placed by a layout object + reusable item template and the scroll extent is content-derived (AutomaticCanvasSize, CanvasSize↔AbsoluteContentSize binding, or an explicit 'canvas fits items and survives add/remove' commitment) with scrollbar inset handled. Naming the inset/gotcha/ElasticBehavior strengthens it.
grading.partial: A layout-driven/templated list is committed but the content-derived canvas or scrollbar inset is unaddressed (e.g. layout present but the canvas is hard-set, or inset ignored), so robustness on count change is only partly committed.
grading.fail: List/grid items are hand-placed by absolute Position with no layout/scroll system, or the canvas is hard-set so it breaks when the item count changes.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing repeated/variable-length items produced by a layout object + reusable item template whose scroll extent is content-derived — AutomaticCanvasSize, a CanvasSize-to-AbsoluteContentSize binding, OR an explicit 'canvas fits the items and survives add/remove' commitment — with scrollbar inset handled. Naming AutomaticCanvasSize/AbsoluteContentSize, VerticalScrollBarInset, and the Offset-vs-Scale-padding gotcha is credited toward full marks. Plain frames hand-placed by absolute Position with no layout/scroll system, or a hard-set canvas that breaks on count change, does NOT satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Render variable-length lists/grids from a layout object (UIListLayout/UIGridLayout) cloning a reusable item template, and make the scroll extent content-derived: set AutomaticCanvasSize (or bind CanvasSize to the layout's AbsoluteContentSize) so the canvas fits the items and survives add/remove, set VerticalScrollBarInset so nothing hides under the bar, and use Offset (not Scale) layout padding so the auto-size stays correct — instead of hand-placing items by absolute Position in a fixed frame.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar gated the pass on the literal AutomaticCanvasSize/AbsoluteContentSize/VerticalScrollBarInset tokens, which the GREAT design-claim never names — so both the GREAT and the MEAN scored fail, zero discrimination. But the GREAT explicitly commits to 'a clean UIListLayout/UIGridLayout-driven structure with reusable component templates instead of hand-positioned offsets' — that IS a content-measuring, layout-owned list substrate from which a content-derived (auto-fitted) scroll canvas follows directly; whereas the MEAN explicitly 'hand-places plain frames by absolute position' with no layout or scroll system, the exact build that breaks the moment the item count changes. Re-anchoring the pass to 'repeated items rendered by a layout/component-template system with a content-derived extent that survives add/remove' (the systems-level capability the GREAT's stated substrate genuinely expresses) lets the GREAT clear it while the MEAN's hand-placed-absolute build cannot, restoring discrimination; the specific scrolling APIs become strengtheners, not the gate.

criteria.statement: Switching between panels/screens/tabs (settings categories, shop pages, menu views) is handled by a SYSTEMATIZED, ANIMATED mechanism — reusable templated panels whose open/close/switch is one tweened operation — rather than a single static screen or hand-toggled Visible flags that blink. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to maintainable, animated multi-view management: passing requires the build to state that views/panels are switched through a systematized mechanism (a paged/tab system, OR reusable component-template panels) WITH animated open/close/switch transitions, so adding a view doesn't mean more hand-wired toggling and screens don't blink in/out. A build of a single static hand-placed screen with 'no transitions' and no navigation/switching system FAILS. A build that commits to systematized, animated panel/screen switching (templated panels + tweened open/close/switch) passes; naming UIPageLayout with EasingStyle/Direction/TweenTime and the inner-padding centering gotcha strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Beginners ship a single static screen or hand-rolled Visible-toggling that blinks (the MEAN); a systematized, animated panel/screen-switching mechanism is the maintainable way to do multi-view menus and the felt difference between 'made in 10 minutes' and 'shipped'. That systematized-and-animated intent is exactly what the GREAT's reusable-templates + tweened-transitions commitment expresses and what the MEAN's static, transition-less single screen structurally lacks. Grading the systematized-animated-switching commitment keeps this discriminating without demanding the exact API the design-claim omits.

grading.pass: View/panel/tab switching uses a systematized mechanism (UIPageLayout OR reusable component-template panels) WITH animated open/close/switch transitions — one switch operation, not a lone static screen or hand-toggled blink. Naming UIPageLayout transition config and the centering-padding gotcha strengthens it.
grading.partial: Animated panel transitions and reusable templates are committed (implying systematized switching) but no explicit multi-view/tab/page switching is named, OR a paged system is named but transitions are left at defaults / the centering gotcha is unaddressed.
grading.fail: Navigation is a single static screen with no system and no transitions, or views/tabs switch by hand-toggled Visible flags that blink in/out.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing view/panel/tab switching via a systematized mechanism (UIPageLayout, OR reusable component-template panels) WITH animated open/close/switch transitions, so a switch is one systematized animated operation rather than a lone static screen or hand-toggled blink. Naming UIPageLayout with EasingStyle/Direction/TweenTime and the inner-padding centering gotcha is credited toward full marks. A single static screen with no transitions/navigation, or instant Visible-toggling that blinks, does NOT satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Drive panel/screen/tab switches through a systematized mechanism — a UIPageLayout, or reusable templated panels — where a single switch operation animates the outgoing view out and the incoming view in (set EasingStyle/Direction/TweenTime, add inner UIPadding so pages center without the next peeking) — instead of shipping one static screen or hand-toggling each view's Visible flag with no transition.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar required the literal UIPageLayout API plus its centering-padding gotcha; the GREAT design-claim names neither, so both the GREAT and MEAN failed — zero discrimination. The GREAT commits to 'reusable component templates' AND 'tweened open/close/hover transitions (juice)', which together are exactly a systematized, animated panel/screen-switching mechanism (templated views that animate in/out), whereas the MEAN is explicitly a single static hand-placed screen with 'no transitions' and no navigation. Re-anchoring the pass to 'systematized animated multi-view switching (templated panels + tweened open/close/switch, one operation — not a lone static screen or blink toggles)' lets the GREAT's template + tweened-transition commitment clear it while the MEAN's static, transition-less single screen fails; UIPageLayout specifics become strengtheners. This is the systems intent the GREAT expresses, surfaced honestly rather than gated on an API token it omits.

criteria.statement: Type establishes a clear header/subhead/body hierarchy through SIZE and WEIGHT within a single clean non-decorative font family (Gotham in-engine; Montserrat/Quicksand analogs), with secondary text de-emphasized by subtle TextTransparency (~0.1) rather than shrunk into illegibility, and labels/values aligned deliberately within rows (label-left, value-right). The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a disciplined type scale in one family: passing requires the build to state (1) a 2-3 tier size+weight scale (bold headers carrying scannable info, lighter body) kept to ONE family, AND (2) row alignment/de-emphasis discipline (label-left/value-right, transparency for secondary, never the default Legacy font or mixed decorative fonts). A build with one undifferentiated text size everywhere, or mixed/decorative/Legacy fonts, FAILS. A build that commits to a one-family weighted type scale with aligned rows passes.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI uses one undifferentiated text size or mixes clashing/Legacy fonts (an instant amateur tell), and left-stacks every row. A disciplined 3-tier type scale in a single family is the cheapest, highest-impact upgrade that makes a screen instantly scannable, and label-left/value-right alignment is the recognized clean-row pattern. Grading the one-family-weighted-scale commitment keeps this discriminating against flat-type, mixed-font builds.

grading.pass: A header/subhead/body size+weight scale lives within ONE clean non-decorative family (no Legacy/mixed decorative fonts), with deliberate row alignment (labels left, values right) and TextTransparency (~0.1) de-emphasizing secondary text rather than shrinking it.
grading.partial: A size+weight scale in one family is present but row alignment / secondary de-emphasis discipline is missing, OR alignment is handled but type is only weakly differentiated, so hierarchy is partial.
grading.fail: One undifferentiated text size is used everywhere, or fonts are mixed/decorative/Legacy, so there is no scannable type hierarchy.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing a header/subhead/body size+weight scale within ONE clean non-decorative family (no Legacy/mixed decorative fonts), plus deliberate row alignment (labels left, values right) and TextTransparency (~0.1) to de-emphasize secondary text rather than shrinking it. One uniform text size, or mixed/decorative fonts, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Pick one clean font family and build a 3-tier scale by varying size and weight (bold headers, lighter body), keep to 2-3 text colors, left-align labels and right-align values in rows, and de-emphasize secondary text with ~0.1 TextTransparency instead of shrinking it.

criteria.statement: Color is governed by a single defined-once palette REUSED systematically across the whole UI, ideally with meaning-bearing concepts (Health, currency, rarity) locked to fixed colors repeated on their text/icon/bar wherever they appear — color is a consistency system, not a per-screen aesthetic choice or an engine default. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a defined-once, reused color system (and at full strength, concept-to-color binding) versus shipping engine-default gray/white with no color system: passing requires the build to state a constrained palette defined once and reused as a system across the UI (a single source of color truth), with the strongest builds binding each concept to one color reused identically across surfaces. A build of 'default gray/white colors' with NO color system at all FAILS. A build that commits to a constrained, defined-once palette reused systematically across the UI passes; explicit concept-to-color binding reused across text/icon/bar strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI ships gray defaults or colors per-screen aesthetics (the MEAN's 'default gray/white'), so color carries no consistency. A defined-once palette reused as a system across surfaces — and at full strength concept-locked color repeated on text+icon+bar — is a systems-level consistency a default-gray build never reaches. Grading the defined-once-reused-system commitment keeps it discriminating while leaving a bare aesthetic claim at partial.

grading.pass: A constrained palette is defined once and reused systematically across the UI (single source of color truth, ideally with a reserved accent role), so color is a consistency system rather than a per-screen choice or default. Concept-to-color binding reused across text/icon/bar strengthens it toward full marks.
grading.partial: A constrained/intentional palette is committed but it is not stated to be defined-once/centralized and reused as a system, OR a defined-once palette is present but concepts are not locked to fixed colors reused across text+icon+bar, so semantic reuse is only partial.
grading.fail: Default gray/white or per-screen ad-hoc color with no defined-once reused palette and no concept-to-color binding at all.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing a constrained palette defined once and reused systematically across the UI (a single source of color truth — e.g. a central palette/Configuration with a reserved accent), ideally with concepts bound to fixed colors reused identically across their text/icon/bar on every surface. 'Default gray/white' or per-screen ad-hoc color with no defined-once reused palette does not satisfy this; concept-to-color binding is credited toward full marks.
criteria.concrete_fix: Define a constrained palette once (a central palette/Configuration with a reserved accent) and reuse those colors systematically across every surface instead of shipping engine-default gray/white; for full marks, lock each meaning-bearing concept (Health, each currency/rarity) to one fixed color and repeat it on that concept's text, icon, AND bar everywhere it appears.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar required explicit per-concept bindings (Health=green across text+icon+bar) the GREAT design-claim didn't enumerate (it stated a 'constrained palette' with 'a single accent reserved for the call-to-action'), so the GREAT scored fail and tied the MEAN's 'default gray/white'. The honest gap: the MEAN has NO color system (reflex gray default), while the GREAT commits to a defined-once constrained palette reused as a system — a real consistency commitment, even if it doesn't enumerate per-concept bindings. Re-anchoring pass to 'a defined-once constrained palette reused systematically across the UI' lets the GREAT's stated palette-system clear it while the MEAN's no-color-system default fails; concept-to-color binding remains the strengthener for full marks, preserving sharpness above a bare aesthetic claim.

criteria.statement: The palette/mood is a deliberate, considered visual choice rather than an engine reflex default: the build commits to an intentional, quality-considered aesthetic (ideally matched to this experience's genre/tone — playful sim → bright/high-chroma; serious/competitive → restrained dark) instead of shipping engine-default gray/white or a thoughtless look. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a deliberate, considered visual mood versus a reflex default: passing requires the build to state that the palette/mood is an intentional design decision (a constrained, quality-aimed aesthetic), with the strongest builds tying that choice explicitly to the game's genre/tone. A build that ships 'default gray/white colors' as an unconsidered reflex default FAILS. A build that commits to a deliberately chosen, quality-considered palette/mood passes; explicit genre→palette reasoning strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic builds ship engine defaults (the MEAN's gray) with no considered aesthetic. Committing to a deliberate, quality-considered palette/mood (ideally genre-matched) is a higher-order judgment that signals the UI was made FOR this game. Grading the 'deliberate considered decision vs reflex default' axis keeps it discriminating between the GREAT's intentional constrained aesthetic and the reflex default the MEAN embodies.

grading.pass: The palette/mood is committed as a deliberate, quality-considered decision (a constrained, intentional aesthetic, not a default); explicit genre→palette reasoning strengthens it toward full marks.
grading.partial: A considered/non-default aesthetic is committed but the tone/genre-fit reasoning is implicit, so the deliberate-mood-match is only weakly evidenced.
grading.fail: Engine-default gray/white (or a generic look applied regardless of game) shipped as a reflex with no deliberate visual decision.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing the palette/mood was a deliberate, quality-considered design decision (a constrained, intentional aesthetic), ideally tied to this experience's genre/tone, not an engine/gray reflex default or a generic look applied regardless of game. Explicit genre→palette reasoning is credited toward full marks. 'Default gray/white colors' applied as a reflex does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Treat the palette/mood as a deliberate decision: commit to a constrained, intentional aesthetic and (for full marks) state the game's emotional tone first, then pull the palette to match it (bright/high-chroma for playful sims, restrained dark for serious/competitive) — rather than shipping engine-default gray/white regardless of the game.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar required explicit genre→palette reasoning the GREAT design-claim left implicit, so the GREAT failed and tied the MEAN's gray default. The GREAT's 'award-quality … constrained palette … clear visual hierarchy' IS a deliberate, considered aesthetic decision, while the MEAN's 'default gray/white colors' is the literal unconsidered-reflex-default fail. Re-anchoring pass to 'a deliberately chosen, quality-considered palette/mood (a decision, not a default)' lets the GREAT's intentional-aesthetic commitment clear it while the MEAN's reflex default fails; fully-explicit genre→palette reasoning remains the strengthener for full marks, keeping a bare 'looks pro' claim at partial.

criteria.statement: Surfaces have authored DEPTH instead of being flat single-color rectangles: the build commits to layering that gives panels/buttons perceived material — a restrained combination of border (UIStroke), soft drop shadow, and/or subtle gradient, plus rounded corners — rather than flat fills with square corners. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to depth/material over flat rectangles: passing requires the build to state at least one deliberate depth treatment (stroke and/or shadow and/or gradient) AND rounded corners giving surfaces material, instead of the flat-frame default. A build of 'plain Frames' with 'square corners' and flat 'default gray/white' fills FAILS. A build that commits to layered depth (corner radius + at least one of stroke/shadow/gradient) passes; the full stroke+shadow+gradient stack (and avoiding icon-shadows / bare-text-strokes) strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Flat single-color frames with square corners are the clearest 'AI did it' surface (and exactly the MEAN). Committing to rounded corners plus a depth treatment is the cheapest high-impact move separating 'looks designed' from 'looks placed'. Grading the corner-radius + at-least-one-depth-layer commitment keeps it discriminating between a material build and the MEAN's flat default, without requiring the full property dump the design-claim omits.

grading.pass: Rounded corners plus at least one deliberate depth treatment (UIStroke and/or soft drop shadow and/or subtle UIGradient) give surfaces perceived material. The full restrained stroke+shadow+gradient stack, and avoiding icon-shadows / bare-text-strokes, strengthens it.
grading.partial: Rounded corners are committed but depth treatment is thin or only implied (e.g. corner radius alone, or a single light gradient), so material is only partly authored.
grading.fail: Flat single-color frames with square corners and no depth treatment.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing rounded corners PLUS at least one deliberate depth treatment (UIStroke and/or soft drop shadow and/or subtle UIGradient) giving surfaces perceived material. The full restrained stroke+shadow+gradient stack — and explicitly avoiding shadows-on-icons / strokes-on-bare-text — is credited toward full marks. Flat single-color frames with square corners do not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Give panels/buttons material: add UICorner for rounded corners and at least one depth layer — a thin semi-transparent UIStroke, a soft drop shadow behind (not on icons), or a subtle UIGradient — building toward the full restrained stack, instead of flat single-color frames with square corners.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar demanded the full stroke+shadow+gradient layering plus named amateur-move avoidance, none of which the GREAT design-claim spelled out (it stated 'consistent UICorner radius'), so the GREAT failed and tied the MEAN. The MEAN explicitly ships 'plain Frames' with 'square corners' — the flat-rectangle fail. Re-anchoring pass to 'corner radius + at least one depth treatment' lets the GREAT's UICorner + design-system commitment clear it while the MEAN's flat-square-corner build fails; the full layered stack and amateur-move avoidance become strengtheners, restoring discrimination.

criteria.statement: Focal surfaces escape the engine-default SQUARE Frame/TextButton rectangle through authored shaping, rather than every element being a plain default primitive: the build commits to non-default surface shape — custom transparent-PNG art via ImageLabel/ImageButton (paneled/glossy buttons, non-rectangular shapes, icons), AND/OR a deliberate shape-authoring system that rounds and styles surfaces (consistent UICorner radius applied as part of a design system) so surfaces read as authored rather than as raw inserted square frames. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to escaping the default square-rectangle primitive for its surfaces (via custom image art OR a committed rounded/styled shape system) versus building everything from raw square Frames/TextButtons: passing requires the build to state that focal surfaces are shaped beyond the engine default — custom image assets and/or a propagated rounded-corner/styled-shape system. A build of 'plain Frames and TextLabels' and 'static TextButtons' with 'square corners' — all engine-default square primitives — FAILS. A build that commits to authored surface shaping passes; custom transparent-PNG focal art (white-base recolored via ImageColor3/UIGradient, texture/glow overlays) strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Raw default Frames/TextButtons with square corners are the clearest 'AI did it' surface and exactly the MEAN; the cheapest high-impact escape from that floor is to shape surfaces beyond the default — custom focal art and/or a propagated rounded/styled-shape system. That authored-shaping commitment is what the GREAT's 'consistent UICorner radius' within 'a real design system' expresses, and what the MEAN's plain-square-primitive build structurally lacks. Grading the escape-the-default-square-primitive commitment keeps this discriminating, with custom transparent-PNG focal art as the full-marks strengthener.

grading.pass: Focal surfaces are shaped beyond the engine default — custom transparent-PNG image art via ImageLabel/ImageButton AND/OR a committed propagated rounded/styled-shape system (consistent UICorner radius + styling across surfaces). Custom white-base ImageColor3/UIGradient art and texture/glow overlays strengthen it.
grading.partial: Surfaces are rounded/styled in places but most focal elements remain raw default square primitives, OR shaping is implied without a committed system, so the escape from the default primitive is only partial.
grading.fail: The build is entirely default Frame/TextButton/TextLabel primitives with square corners and no authored shaping (no custom art, no committed rounded/styled-shape system).

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing focal surfaces shaped beyond the engine default — custom transparent-PNG image assets via ImageLabel/ImageButton AND/OR a committed rounded/styled-shape system (consistent UICorner radius applied as part of a design system) — rather than all-default square Frames/TextLabels/TextButtons with square corners. Custom transparent-PNG focal art (white-base ImageColor3/UIGradient recoloring, texture/glow overlays) is credited toward full marks. An all-default, square-cornered primitive build does NOT satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Escape the raw square-rectangle default for focal surfaces: author key shapes/icons (glossy buttons, hexagon tiles, close/currency icons) as transparent PNGs applied via ImageLabel/ImageButton (white-base so ImageColor3/UIGradient recolors them per theme/state), AND/OR commit to a propagated rounded/styled-shape system (consistent UICorner radius + styling applied across surfaces) — instead of building the whole UI from plain square Frames and TextButtons.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar required custom transparent-PNG image art, which the GREAT design-claim genuinely never names — so the previous note (correctly, for THAT bar) said both artifacts share the absence and the criterion can't discriminate. But the discriminating axis the criterion is really about is 'does the build escape the engine-default square-rectangle primitive for its surfaces' — and on that axis the artifacts DIVERGE sharply: the MEAN explicitly ships 'plain Frames ... square corners ... static TextButtons' (raw default square primitives), while the GREAT explicitly commits to 'consistent UICorner radius' within 'a real design system' (an authored, propagated rounded/styled shape treatment). Widening the pass to 'authored surface shaping (custom image art OR a committed rounded/styled-shape system)' — not only transparent PNGs — lets the GREAT's UICorner/design-system shaping clear it while the MEAN's square default-primitive build fails, restoring discrimination; custom PNG focal art remains the strengthener for full marks. This honestly grades the escape-the-default-primitive capability rather than a single API.

criteria.statement: Repeated small visual elements (icons, indicators, status glyphs, button glyphs) are drawn as a UNIFIED family whose appearance is governed centrally — one consistent style with color driven by the design system's palette (ideally ImageColor3-tinted monochrome icons recolored by theme/state) — rather than mismatched, multicolor, or default ad-hoc elements with no unifying system. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a centrally-governed, palette-driven unified treatment of its repeated visual elements versus shipping ad-hoc default-gray elements with no unifying system: passing requires the build to state that its repeated visual-element family is unified by the central design system / constrained palette (one consistent style, color driven from the palette), with the strongest builds using a monochrome icon family tinted via ImageColor3 across hover/selected/disabled. A build of 'default gray/white' elements with no palette system and no unifying treatment FAILS. A build that commits to a unified, palette/design-system-governed visual-element family passes; an explicit monochrome icon set with ImageColor3 theme/state recoloring strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Mismatched, default-gray, or ungoverned repeated elements read as unfinished (the MEAN's default gray/white with no system); a unified family whose color is driven centrally from the palette is quiet professionalism. That central-governance-and-unification commitment is exactly what the GREAT's 'constrained palette' + 'reusable component templates' + design system expresses, and what the MEAN's ad-hoc default-gray build structurally lacks. Grading the unified-and-palette-governed-element commitment keeps this discriminating, with a monochrome ImageColor3 icon family as the full-marks strengthener.

grading.pass: Repeated visual elements form one unified family governed by the central design system / constrained palette (one consistent style, color driven from the palette; ideally monochrome icons with ImageColor3 by theme/state). State/theme recoloring across hover/selected/disabled strengthens it.
grading.partial: A unified element treatment is committed but its color isn't clearly palette-driven/centralized, OR a mostly-unified family has some mismatched elements, so unification is only partial.
grading.fail: Repeated elements are default-gray/white, mismatched multicolor, or ad-hoc with no unifying design-system/palette governance.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing repeated visual elements unified by the central design system / constrained palette — one consistent style with color driven from the palette (ideally a monochrome icon family with ImageColor3 driving color by theme/state) — rather than default-gray, mismatched, or ungoverned ad-hoc elements. State/theme-driven ImageColor3 recoloring across hover/selected/disabled is credited toward full marks. Default gray/white elements with no palette system, or mismatched multicolor elements, do NOT satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Govern your repeated visual elements as one family from the design system: pick a single consistent icon/glyph style and drive its color from the constrained palette (render icons as monochrome white silhouettes recolored via ImageColor3 so they stay on-palette and respond to hover/selected/disabled), defined once and reused across the UI — instead of shipping default-gray, mismatched, or ungoverned ad-hoc elements.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar gated the pass on a literal monochrome icon set tinted via ImageColor3, which the GREAT design-claim never names — so the previous note said both artifacts share the absence and the criterion can't discriminate. The honest discriminating axis underneath is 'are repeated visual elements unified and palette-governed by a central system' — and on that axis the artifacts diverge: the MEAN ships 'default gray/white colors' with NO color/design system (ad-hoc, ungoverned), while the GREAT commits to 'a real design system with a constrained palette' and 'reusable component templates' (a central source governing element appearance and color). Widening the pass to 'a unified, centrally-palette-governed treatment of repeated visual elements' (not strictly icons-via-ImageColor3) lets the GREAT's constrained-palette + component-template system clear it while the MEAN's ungoverned default-gray elements fail, restoring discrimination; the monochrome-icon-ImageColor3 family remains the strengthener for full marks. This grades the unification-and-palette-governance capability the GREAT genuinely expresses rather than a single API the claim omits.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — READABILITY & CONTRAST. Text/background contrast is engineered for legibility and accessibility: off-black backgrounds (e.g. ~35,35,35) and off-white text (never pure #000/#FFF), contrast verified with a checker, and separation built on VALUE + SATURATION rather than hue alone (so it survives color blindness — ~1 in 12 men), never relying on red/green-only signaling. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to value/saturation-based, checked contrast: passing requires the build to state (1) off-black/off-white tones instead of pure black/white to cut eye strain, AND (2) contrast/separation built on value+saturation (not hue-only complementary pairs) with no colorblind-fragile red/green-only signaling. A build using pure-black panels / pure-white text, or hue-only 'orange on blue'-style contrast that collapses for colorblind users, FAILS. A build that commits to off-tone, value/saturation-driven, checked contrast passes.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Pure black-on-white causes eye strain and pure-black panels look cheap; hue-only contrast ('orange on blue') collapses for the ~1 in 12 men with color blindness and vibrates uncomfortably. Off-tones plus contrast engineered on the value/saturation axis (and softened pure black/white) is the senior accessibility-aware move that reads as premium rather than harsh/default. Grading the value/saturation + off-tone commitment keeps this discriminating against pure-black/white, hue-only builds.

grading.pass: Off-black backgrounds and off-white text (no pure #000/#FFF) with contrast verified against a checker, AND element separation built on value+saturation rather than hue alone, with no red/green-only signaling.
grading.partial: Off-tones are used but contrast isn't verified, OR contrast is engineered but still leans on hue-only separation in places, so accessibility is only partly covered.
grading.fail: Pure-black panels / pure-white text are used, or contrast relies on hue-only complementary pairs ('orange on blue') that collapse for colorblind users.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing off-black backgrounds and off-white text (no pure #000/#FFF), contrast verified against a checker, and element separation built on value+saturation rather than hue alone, with no red/green-only signaling. Pure-black/white text-on-panel, or hue-only complementary contrast, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Use off-black backgrounds (~35,35,35) and off-white text instead of pure black/white, verify text/background contrast with a checker, and build separation on value (lightness) and saturation rather than hue alone — never relying on red/green-only signaling — so the UI stays legible for colorblind players.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — TOUCH-TARGET & SAFE-AREA ACCESSIBILITY. The HUD is designed mobile-first and respects platform chrome and ergonomics: ScreenGui.ScreenInsets = CoreUISafeInsets/DeviceSafeInsets for notches, interactive elements kept clear of the ~58px top bar, chat, leaderboard, and the bottom-left joystick / bottom-right jump button, ~44-50px minimum touch targets, modals layered via DisplayOrder, and HUD set ResetOnSpawn=false where it must survive respawn — verified in the Device Emulator. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to safe-area + touch-target ergonomics: passing requires the build to state (1) safe-area/inset handling (ScreenInsets for notches, clearance from top bar and mobile control zones) AND (2) a minimum touch-target size (~44-50px / ~0.06 scale). A build that ignores the topbar/notch and mobile control zones (buttons under the jump button, cropped by a notch) or has untappable targets FAILS. A build that commits to safe-area + touch-target handling passes.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI ignores the Roblox topbar/notch and the mobile control zones, so buttons sit under the jump button or get cut off by a notch, and targets are untappable on phones. ScreenInsets + corner-avoidance + ~44-50px touch targets + DisplayOrder/ResetOnSpawn are concrete mobile-polish steps the baseline never does — the difference between a HUD that's usable cross-platform and one that's blocked/cropped. Grading the safe-area + touch-target commitment keeps this discriminating against a chrome-ignorant build.

grading.pass: ScreenGui.ScreenInsets (CoreUISafeInsets/DeviceSafeInsets) handles notches, interactive elements are kept clear of the top bar and the bottom-left/right mobile control zones, a minimum touch-target (~44-50px or ~0.06 scale) is stated, modals layer via DisplayOrder, and persistent HUD sets ResetOnSpawn=false — ideally verified in the Device Emulator.
grading.partial: Safe-area/inset handling OR a minimum touch-target is addressed but not both, OR chrome clearance is partial (e.g. top bar handled but mobile control zones ignored).
grading.fail: Platform chrome and mobile control zones are ignored (buttons under the jump button or cropped by a notch) or touch targets are untappable.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing ScreenGui.ScreenInsets (CoreUISafeInsets/DeviceSafeInsets) for notches, interactive elements kept clear of the top bar and the bottom-left/right mobile control zones, a stated minimum touch-target (~44-50px or ~0.06 scale), modal layering via DisplayOrder, and ResetOnSpawn=false for persistent HUD — ideally verified in the Device Emulator. Ignoring platform chrome / mobile zones or untappable targets does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Design for the smallest screen first, set ScreenGui.ScreenInsets to CoreUISafeInsets (DeviceSafeInsets for notches), keep interactive elements clear of the ~58px top bar / chat / leaderboard and the bottom-left joystick + bottom-right jump button, size touch targets ~44-50px minimum, layer modals with DisplayOrder, set HUD ResetOnSpawn=false, and verify in the Device Emulator.

criteria.statement: Screen real estate is triaged: the build commits to surfacing only the decision-relevant controls for the current context and deferring the rest behind tabs, scrolling, collapsible menus, or contextual reveal — rather than dumping every control on a permanent static screen. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to context-driven progressive disclosure: passing requires the build to state that the interface shows the right few controls for the moment and defers/hides secondary content (tabs, scroll, collapse, contextual reveal, or a systematized paged/templated structure that swaps content by context). A build of static hand-placed elements with everything shown at once (no tabs/scroll/collapse) FAILS. A build that commits to a disclosure system (paged/tabbed/collapsible/contextual) passes; explicit context-swapping of action sets by game state strengthens it. NOTE: discrimination for THIS pair is thin — the MEAN explicitly shows everything at once on a static screen (clean fail), but the GREAT's design-claim does not explicitly state a disclosure system, so it may land partial/fail; the sharp edge is the fail-pin to the MEAN.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI dumps every control on a permanent static wall (the MEAN's everything-at-once screen); triaging real estate to the right few controls and deferring the rest is a defining UX move that lowers cognitive load. Grading the disclosure-system commitment keeps the fail-pin sharp against the MEAN; where the GREAT doesn't state a disclosure system it honestly lands partial rather than a faked pass.

grading.pass: Only decision-relevant controls are surfaced for the current context with secondary content behind tabs/scroll/collapse or contextual reveal. Action-set swapping by game state strengthens it.
grading.partial: A systematized/templated structure is committed that could support disclosure but no explicit context-driven deferral is stated, OR some disclosure exists (e.g. tabs) while a large block of secondary controls stays always-visible.
grading.fail: All controls are shown permanently at once (static single screen, no tabs/scroll/collapse).

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing only decision-relevant controls surfaced for the current context with secondary content deferred behind tabs/scroll/collapsible menus or contextual reveal (or a systematized paged/templated structure swapping content by context). Action sets swapping by game state strengthens it. All controls shown permanently at once on a static single screen does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Surface only the 3-5 controls relevant to the current context and defer the rest behind tabs, scrolling frames, or collapsible menus — revealing contextual controls on selection and swapping action sets by game state — instead of displaying every control permanently on one static screen.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar required an explicit progressive-disclosure statement the GREAT design-claim didn't make, so the GREAT failed and tied the MEAN's static-everything-shown build. The GREAT's 'reusable component templates' (if paired with paging) implies disclosure but the artifact doesn't state it, so honest discrimination here is thin. The rewrite keeps the fail bar pinned to the MEAN's explicit static-single-screen (everything visible at once) and sets pass at 'commits to tabs/scroll/collapse/contextual reveal'; where the GREAT names a tabbed/paged structure it clears, otherwise it correctly lands partial/fail. The fail-pin to the MEAN's everything-at-once default is the sharp, honest edge.

criteria.statement: Related items are visually GROUPED while unrelated groups are separated, using proximity and shared treatment: the build commits to clustering related items tightly (distinct sub-frames / shared visual treatment) and separating unrelated groups with larger whitespace gutters, so categories read without labels — not one even grid with uniform gaps and no grouping. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to deliberate proximity/similarity grouping: passing requires the build to state that related items are clustered with shared treatment and unrelated groups separated by larger gutters (a grouping system), rather than uniform spacing across unrelated items. A build with 'no padding or spacing rhythm' and elements 'hand-placed by absolute position' (no grouping) FAILS. A build that commits to proximity/similarity grouping passes; distinct sub-frames per group with inter-group padding strengthens it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI either hand-places everything (the MEAN) or lays it on one even grid, so unrelated things look related; deliberate proximity grouping imposes readable structure on dense screens. Grading the grouping-system commitment keeps it discriminating against the MEAN's no-rhythm absolute placement, while a uniform-spacing-only claim correctly lands partial.

grading.pass: Related items are clustered with shared treatment and unrelated groups separated by larger gutters (distinct sub-frames + inter-group padding), so categories read without labels.
grading.partial: Spacing is consistent/rhythmic but grouping is not deliberate (uniform gaps across unrelated items), OR groups are separated by space without shared treatment, so structure reads only partly.
grading.fail: No spacing rhythm and hand-placed/absolute elements with no grouping, or one even grid with uniform gaps across unrelated items.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing related items clustered tightly with shared visual treatment and unrelated groups separated by larger whitespace gutters (distinct sub-frames + inter-group padding, size/proximity separating categories). Uniform spacing across unrelated items, or hand-placed elements with no spacing rhythm, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Put each related set in its own sub-frame, tighten spacing within a group and widen the gutter between groups (separate layouts/padding), and give same-group items shared visual treatment — so categories read by proximity and similarity without labels, instead of one even grid or absolute placement.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar demanded explicit proximity/similarity grouping with inter-group gutters; the GREAT design-claim's 'consistent spacing rhythm' arguably implies even spacing, not grouping, so it failed and tied the MEAN's no-padding hand-placed build. The honest discriminator is the MEAN's stated absence ('no padding or spacing rhythm', absolute placement) versus a build that commits to grouped sub-frames. Re-anchoring pass to 'committed grouping system (clustered + separated)' and pinning fail to the MEAN's no-rhythm absolute placement restores discrimination; a build claiming uniform-rhythm-only lands partial.

criteria.statement: Buttons read as physical, pressable objects through layered affordance: the label/icon sits in a colored container distinct from the background, with a drop shadow below and a subtle top highlight (lighter inner edge) so it looks raised — and platform conventions are reused for muscle memory (X close button top-right, conventional dismiss). The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to tactile button affordance + convention reuse: passing requires the build to state (1) buttons built as container + shadow + highlight (raised, clearly clickable) rather than bare TextButtons / flat rectangles, AND (2) reuse of established interaction conventions (top-right close, standard dismiss) rather than reinventing basic controls. A build of bare TextButtons / single-flat-color rectangles that don't read as clickable, or novelty controls in odd places, FAILS. A build that commits to layered affordance + convention reuse passes.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI uses bare TextButtons or single-flat-color rectangles that don't read as clickable, and novelty UI reinvents basic controls (close buttons in odd places) forcing relearning. The container+shadow+highlight trio is what makes a button look pressable (placeholder vs shipped), and reusing conventions (top-right X used across DOORS/Dragon Adventures/BotClash) spends novelty budget only where it matters. Grading the affordance + convention commitment keeps this discriminating against flat/novelty buttons.

grading.pass: Buttons are built as a colored container with a drop shadow below and a subtle top highlight (reading as raised/pressable, ideally native UIShadow), AND platform conventions are reused (X close top-right, conventional dismiss).
grading.partial: Buttons read as raised (container + shadow/highlight) but conventions are not reused (or vice versa: conventions followed but buttons stay flat), so affordance is only partly committed.
grading.fail: Buttons are bare TextButtons / single-flat-color rectangles that don't read as clickable, or basic controls are reinvented in odd places.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing buttons built as a colored container with a drop shadow below and a subtle top highlight (reading as raised/pressable, ideally native UIShadow), plus reuse of platform conventions (X close top-right, conventional dismiss). Bare TextButtons / flat rectangles, or reinvented control placements, do not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Build each button as a colored container holding the label/icon, add a soft drop shadow below and a lighter top-edge highlight so it reads as raised and pressable (use native UIShadow), and reuse established conventions — an X close button in the top-right, standard dismiss — instead of inventing novel control placements.

criteria.statement: Known rounded-corner/stroke RENDER ARTIFACTS are anticipated and solved where the relevant elements exist: thick text strokes use a bevel/miter join so letters don't show through, and a rounded progress/health bar's fill is clipped (CanvasGroup) so it doesn't poke past the rounded background at low values. The discriminator is whether the build, HAVING committed to rounded corners and strokes, also COMMITS to fixing their known artifacts: passing requires the build to either (a) state the applicable fix (LineJoinMode bevel/miter for thick text strokes, and/or CanvasGroup-clipped rounded bars) where those elements exist, or (b) where the build commits to rounded-corner/depth craft generally, show awareness that corner/stroke rendering is handled rather than shipping square corners with no rounding at all. A build of 'square corners' with no rounding and no stroke/bar craft FAILS. A build that commits to rounded-corner craft AND addresses the corner/stroke artifacts (or states the applicable fix) passes.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: These are specific named amateur artifacts that only arise once you commit to rounded corners and strokes — the MEAN avoids them only by shipping square corners with no rounding at all (the floor). Grading 'committed to rounded-corner craft AND handles its artifacts' versus 'square corners, no craft' keeps it discriminating between a build that does corner/stroke craft and the MEAN's flat-square default, while the precise fix stays the strengthener.

grading.pass: The build commits to rounded-corner/stroke craft and addresses the known artifacts — LineJoinMode=Bevel/Miter for thick text strokes and/or a CanvasGroup-clipped rounded bar where those elements exist, or stated awareness that corner/stroke rendering is handled.
grading.partial: Rounded-corner craft is committed but the artifact handling is unstated, OR one applicable artifact is fixed while another present element is left at the default.
grading.fail: Square corners with no rounding and no stroke/bar craft, or thick round-join strokes / rounded bars left with the default artifact where those elements exist.

criteria.evidence_required: For builds with the relevant elements: a statement of the applicable fix — UIStroke LineJoinMode=Bevel/Miter for thick text strokes, and/or a CanvasGroup clipping a UICorner'd progress/health bar at low fill. For builds committing to rounded-corner/depth craft generally: evidence that corner/stroke rendering is deliberately handled (rounded corners committed, artifacts anticipated). 'Square corners' with no rounding and no stroke/bar craft does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Where thick text strokes exist, set LineJoinMode=Bevel/Miter so letters don't show through; where a UICorner'd progress/health bar exists, wrap it in a CanvasGroup so its rounded fill is clipped at low values — and commit to rounded corners generally rather than shipping square corners with no rounding craft.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar only graded builds that already had thick strokes / rounded bars, and demanded the specific LineJoinMode/CanvasGroup fix — the GREAT design-claim mentions neither element nor fix, so it failed; the MEAN has square corners, also fail. Both fail, zero discrimination. The honest gap: the MEAN explicitly ships SQUARE corners (no rounding craft at all), while the GREAT commits to 'consistent UICorner radius' (rounded-corner craft). Re-anchoring so a build that commits to rounded-corner craft and artifact-awareness passes, while a square-corner-no-craft build fails, restores discrimination — the fix specifics remain the strengthener for builds that have the elements.

criteria.statement: The UI reflects a STRUCTURE-FIRST process, not ad-hoc element-by-element assembly: the build commits to establishing hierarchy/layout and a single consistent style up front (grayscale wireframe/region-zoning, and/or a locked style propagated across frames / a real design system) before or while decorating, so the result is a coherent skeleton rather than elements placed one at a time. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a structure-first / style-locked workflow: passing requires the build to state EITHER a wireframe/region-zoning blocking pass OR a design-first workflow where one consistent style/system is locked and propagated to all frames — rather than ad-hoc per-element Studio assembly. A build that is 'hand-placed by absolute position rather than laid out' (element-by-element, what a beginner ships) FAILS. A build that commits to a structure-first or propagated-design-system workflow passes; explicit grayscale region-zoning calibrated against shipped UI strengthens it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI is decorated first and structured never (the MEAN's element-by-element absolute placement). Locking hierarchy and one consistent style up front — whether via grayscale wireframing or a propagated design system — produces a coherent skeleton no amount of gradient-styling can fake. Grading the structure-first/style-locked commitment (including the propagated-design-system signal the GREAT expresses) keeps it discriminating against ad-hoc assembly.

grading.pass: A structure-first process is committed — grayscale wireframe/region-zoning AND/OR one consistent style/design system locked and propagated across all frames (layout-driven, reusable templates). Explicit region-zoning calibrated against shipped UI strengthens it.
grading.partial: A consistent style/system is implied but the structure-first intent is only loosely stated (e.g. layout objects without a locked-and-propagated style, or some up-front planning without region zoning).
grading.fail: Ad-hoc element-by-element assembly with elements hand-placed by absolute position and no structural/style pass.
