criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing a structure-first process — grayscale wireframe/region-zoning blocking, AND/OR a design-first workflow where one consistent style/design system is locked and propagated across all frames (layout-driven, reusable templates) rather than per-element placement. Explicit grayscale region-zoning calibrated against shipped top-game UI strengthens it. Ad-hoc element-by-element / absolute-position assembly does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Block the screen in grayscale boxes first (zoning objectives top, gameplay center, controls in thumb zones) and/or lock one consistent style/design system on a sample frame and propagate it to all frames via layout objects and reusable templates — instead of placing elements one at a time by absolute position.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar demanded an explicit grayscale-wireframe or Figma-style-lock workflow statement; the GREAT design-claim described the RESULT ('real design system', 'reusable component templates', layout-driven structure) not the PROCESS, so it failed and tied the MEAN. But 'a real design system … reusable component templates … UIListLayout-driven instead of hand-positioned offsets' IS evidence of one consistent style locked and propagated — a structure-first commitment — whereas the MEAN is explicitly 'hand-placed by absolute position', element-by-element. Re-anchoring pass to accept a propagated-design-system/layout-driven commitment (not only an explicit wireframe narrative) lets the GREAT clear it while the MEAN's ad-hoc placement fails, restoring discrimination.

criteria.statement: Leftover space along a layout axis is distributed by the engine's LAYOUT system rather than faked with hand-coded pixel gaps: the build commits to space being apportioned by a layout object — ideally UIFlex (layout HorizontalFlex/VerticalFlex such as Fill for equal-width tabs; and/or per-child UIFlexItem FlexMode Grow/Fill/Shrink), or at minimum a layout object whose Padding/alignment distributes the gaps — so nav strips fill the width and items space evenly under resize, instead of fixed-offset hand-placed gaps that break when the screen changes. The discriminator is whether spacing/leftover-space is OWNED by a layout system versus hand-coded fixed offsets: passing requires the build to state that gaps/space between siblings are produced by a layout object (UIFlex space distribution preferred; layout-object Padding-driven distribution accepted) rather than per-element fixed-offset placement. A build that hand-places everything by fixed pixel offsets with no layout object FAILS. A build whose space distribution is layout-owned passes; explicit UIFlex (HorizontalFlex/VerticalFlex Fill, UIFlexItem Grow spacer, width-filling tab strip) with dynamic-resize perf-caveat awareness strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic Roblox UI fakes even spacing with hard-coded pixel gaps that break on resize (the MEAN's fixed-offset placement); having the layout system apportion leftover space — width-filling tab strips, Grow spacers, layout-Padding-driven gaps — is the differentiator a fixed-offset build cannot express. The GREAT's 'UIListLayout/UIGridLayout-driven structure' is exactly layout-owned space distribution; the MEAN's fixed offsets are exactly the hand-coded-gap floor. Grading the layout-owned-space-distribution commitment (UIFlex as the full-marks strengthener) keeps this discriminating.

grading.pass: Leftover space is distributed by a layout system — UIFlex (HorizontalFlex/VerticalFlex Fill; UIFlexItem FlexMode Fill/Grow/Shrink) and/or a layout object whose Padding/alignment apportions the gaps so spacing reflows on resize. Explicit UIFlex (Grow spacer / width-filling tab strip) and dynamic-resize perf-caveat awareness strengthen it.
grading.partial: Some space is layout-distributed but key strips/even-spacing elsewhere are still hand-coded fixed offsets, OR layout-Padding distribution is used without UIFlex where width-filling/Grow distribution is clearly wanted.
grading.fail: Even spacing / full-width strips are faked entirely with hand-coded pixel gaps or fixed-offset absolute placement, with no layout object distributing space.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing leftover space distributed by a layout system — UIFlex (layout HorizontalFlex/VerticalFlex e.g. Fill, and/or per-child UIFlexItem FlexMode Grow/Fill/Shrink), OR a layout object whose Padding/alignment apportions the gaps so spacing reflows on resize — rather than hand-coded fixed-offset gaps. Explicit UIFlex (Grow spacer, width-filling tab strip) plus dynamic-resize perf-caveat awareness is credited toward full marks. Fixed pixel-offset placement / hand-coded gaps with no layout object do NOT satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Let the layout distribute space instead of hand-coding gaps: for equal-width tabs set the layout's HorizontalFlex/VerticalFlex to Fill (or add a UIFlexItem FlexMode=Grow spacer between fixed buttons), and at minimum drive all inter-item gaps from a layout object's Padding/alignment so spacing reflows on resize — and avoid flexing without purpose since it costs perf on dynamic resize — instead of fixed pixel-offset placement.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar gated the pass strictly on the UIFlex/UIFlexItem API and explicitly warned that a plain UIListLayout/UIGridLayout 'does not satisfy this' — so the GREAT (which names UIListLayout/UIGridLayout, not UIFlex) failed alongside the MEAN's fixed-offset build, zero discrimination. The real floor this criterion targets is 'space faked with hard-coded pixel gaps' — which is exactly the MEAN ('fixed pixel OFFSETS ... hand-placed by absolute position'), whereas the GREAT explicitly commits to a 'UIListLayout/UIGridLayout-driven structure' where the layout object (via Padding/alignment, and at full strength UIFlex) distributes space, not hand-coded offsets. Re-anchoring the pass to 'leftover space distributed by a layout object (UIFlex preferred, layout-object Padding/alignment distribution accepted)' lets the GREAT's layout-driven space distribution clear it while the MEAN's hand-coded-gap build fails, restoring discrimination; UIFlex specifically remains the strengthener for full marks. This avoids the previous collapse-to-baseline worry by keeping the bar at engine-distributed space (not mere presence of any layout) while honestly crediting the layout-owned distribution the GREAT commits to.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — VISUAL HIERARCHY. One element is made to win the eye by stacking MULTIPLE emphasis signals on it at once — larger area + brighter/more-saturated color + extra surrounding whitespace (UIPadding) + a distinguishing accent (stripe/badge) — while everything else is muted; not a flat grid where every card/button has equal visual weight. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a single-focal-point emphasis stack: passing requires the build to state that ONE featured element (primary CTA, featured gamepass, top bundle) is over-signaled on 2+ axes simultaneously (size AND color AND space/accent) while peers are deliberately de-emphasized. A build that renders every element at equal size/color/weight (uniform grid, same buttons) so the eye has nowhere to land FAILS. A build that commits to a multi-axis focal emphasis stack passes; documented exemplar patterns (enlarged+padded+color-distinguished top bundle; an accent stripe under premium items) strengthen it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic AI UI gives every card/button equal weight — uniform grid, same color, same size — so nothing leads the eye and the screen reads as flat noise; this is named the single biggest tell of intentional design. Award UI picks the ONE thing the player should act on and over-signals it on 3-4 axes at once. Grading the multi-axis-focal-emphasis commitment keeps this discriminating against an equal-weight grid.

grading.pass: ONE featured element (primary CTA, featured gamepass, top bundle) is distinguished on 2+ emphasis axes simultaneously (larger area AND brighter/saturated color AND extra surrounding whitespace and/or an accent stripe/badge) with peers deliberately muted.
grading.partial: One element is emphasized but only on a single axis (e.g. just larger, or just a different color), so it leads weakly rather than via a multi-axis stack.
grading.fail: Every element shares size/color/weight (uniform grid, identical buttons), so the eye has nowhere to land.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing ONE featured element distinguished on 2+ emphasis axes simultaneously (larger area AND brighter/saturated color AND extra surrounding whitespace and/or an accent stripe/badge) with peers muted. A flat layout where all elements share size/color/weight does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Pick the single element the player should act on and stack emphasis on it — enlarge its area, raise its color saturation, give it extra surrounding UIPadding, and add a distinguishing accent stripe/badge — while muting every other element's size and color so the eye lands on the one you chose.

criteria.statement: Visual design is CENTRALIZED so a restyle/theme is a single change, not per-instance edits: the build commits to a central style source — a StyleSheet of StyleRules with selectors and $-tokens + Themes, OR an equivalent code-side token/component style system (reusable component templates whose style is defined once and propagated) — rather than the same colors/corners copy-pasted onto every instance. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a centralized, token/component-driven style system: passing requires the build to state that styling lives in one place and is reused across the UI (StyleSheet/tokens/Themes, or a real design-system of reusable templates with a single style source), so changing the look is one change. A build of per-element default placement with engine-default properties copied per instance FAILS. A build that commits to a centralized style/design-token/component system passes; a full StyleSheet selector+token+Theme architecture strengthens it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI copy-pastes identical (or default) properties onto every instance, so restyling is a manual slog and themes are impossible. A central token/component style source — whether a StyleSheet or a real design system of reusable templates — is design-system-grade and far above the MEAN's per-instance defaults. Grading the centralization commitment (accepting the design-system altitude the GREAT expresses) keeps it discriminating against per-instance duplication.

grading.pass: Styling is centralized and reused — a StyleSheet/StyleRule system with selectors + $-tokens + Themes, or an equivalent real design system of reusable templates with a single style source — so a restyle/theme is one change. A full selector+token+Theme architecture strengthens it.
grading.partial: A partial central source exists (some shared templates or a token table) but many properties are still per-instance, so a restyle is only partly centralized.
grading.fail: The same colors/corners (or engine defaults) are applied per instance with no central style source, so a restyle is a manual slog.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing centralized styling reused across the UI — a StyleSheet/StyleRule system with selectors + $-tokens + Themes, OR an equivalent real design system of reusable component templates whose style is defined once and propagated — so a theme/restyle is a single change. A full selector+token+Theme architecture strengthens it. Per-instance copy-pasted/engine-default properties on each element do not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Centralize styling: define a StyleSheet of StyleRules (selectors + $-tokens + light/dark Themes), or at minimum a real design system of reusable component templates with a single style source, so colors/corners/spacing are defined once and a restyle is one change — instead of copy-pasting properties (or engine defaults) onto every instance.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar demanded a literal StyleSheet/StyleRule/$-token/Theme architecture and explicitly rejected 'reusable component templates' as insufficient — but the GREAT design-claim's 'a real design system' with 'reusable component templates' IS a central style commitment, just expressed at the design altitude, so it failed and tied the MEAN's per-instance-default build. Re-anchoring pass to accept either a StyleSheet/token system OR an equivalent real-design-system-of-reusable-templates-with-single-style-source lets the GREAT's design-system commitment clear it while the MEAN's copy-pasted-defaults build fails; the full StyleSheet selector/Theme stack becomes the strengthener, restoring discrimination.

criteria.statement: Depth is a consistent ELEVATION SYSTEM, not a uniformly flat layer: the build commits to depth cues that map to layer importance — shadows (ideally native UIShadow with tuned blur/offset/spread) that grow softer/larger for higher layers (HUD low, panels mid, modals high), and/or per-corner UICorner radii for distinctive shapes — rather than every element on one flat z=0 plane with square corners. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to an elevation language (depth mapped to importance) versus a uniformly-flat layer: passing requires the build to state shadows/depth used as a consistent elevation system across HUD/panel/modal tiers. A build that is uniformly flat ('plain Frames', 'square corners', every element at one layer) FAILS. A build that commits to an elevation/shadow-tier system passes; native UIShadow with tuned blur/offset/spread per tier and per-corner radii strengthen it. NOTE: discrimination for THIS pair is partial — the MEAN is explicitly uniformly flat with square corners (clean fail), but the GREAT commits only to 'consistent UICorner radius' without naming a shadow elevation tier, so it may land partial; the sharp edge is the fail-pin to the MEAN's flat square-corner plane.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI is uniformly flat — every layer at z=0, square corners, no stacking (the MEAN). An elevation system where shadow size maps to layer importance is how real design systems communicate layering. Grading the elevation-language commitment (shadows-by-importance and/or per-corner radii) keeps the fail-pin sharp against the MEAN's flat plane; where the GREAT commits only to corner radius it honestly lands partial rather than a faked pass.

grading.pass: Depth is a consistent elevation language — shadows (ideally native UIShadow, tuned) mapped to layer importance across HUD/panel/modal, and/or per-corner UICorner radii. Native UIShadow tuned per tier strengthens it.
grading.partial: Some depth/rounding is committed (e.g. consistent UICorner radius) but not as a tiered elevation system (uniform corner radius without a shadow/elevation language mapping depth to importance), so layering is only partly communicated.
grading.fail: Uniformly flat (every element at one z=0 layer, square corners, no elevation cues), or duplicate-frame/9-slice shadow hacks only.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing depth used as a consistent elevation language — shadows (ideally native UIShadow with tuned blur/offset/spread/transparency) mapped so size grows with layer importance across HUD/panel/modal, and/or per-corner UICorner radii for distinctive shapes — not a single uniformly-flat layer. Native UIShadow tuned per tier and per-corner radii strengthen it. A uniformly flat z=0 UI with square corners does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Adopt depth as an elevation scale — small soft shadow on HUD, larger softer on panels, largest on modals — ideally via native UIShadow (tuned BlurRadius/Offset/Spread/Transparency per tier), and use per-corner UICorner radii for distinctive shapes, instead of leaving every element on one flat plane with square corners.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar demanded native UIShadow specifically as a tuned elevation language — the GREAT design-claim names 'consistent UICorner radius + UIPadding' but no UIShadow, so it failed and tied the MEAN's flat build. This is partly a true gap (the GREAT doesn't commit to a shadow elevation tier). The rewrite widens the discriminator from 'native UIShadow tuned per tier' to 'depth as a consistent elevation system (shadows mapped to importance, and/or per-corner radii)', so a build committing to layered depth + tiered elevation clears it while the MEAN's explicitly uniformly-flat square-corner build fails. Where the GREAT commits only to corner radius without an elevation tier it correctly lands partial — but the fail-pin to the MEAN's flat plane is now sharp.

criteria.statement: Resizable surfaces (panels, buttons, frames) hold crisp corners and undistorted proportions across sizes via a scale-aware surface system, rather than fixed-size sprites or fixed-offset square frames that stretch/break when the screen changes: the build commits to surfaces that survive resizing — ideally 9-slice custom art (ImageLabel/ImageButton ScaleType=Slice with SliceCenter/SliceScale so corners stay crisp, edges stretch on one axis, center fills), OR an equivalent scale-aware surface treatment (scale-driven layout + UIAspectRatioConstraint holding proportion + UICorner radius that stays consistent across sizes). The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to surfaces that hold corner-crispness/proportion under resize versus fixed-offset square frames that distort: passing requires the build to state a scale-aware resizable-surface system — 9-slice, OR scale-driven sizing with aspect/proportion held and consistent rounded corners. A build of fixed pixel-offset 'square corners' frames that 'break on other screen sizes' FAILS. A build that commits to scale-aware resizable surfaces passes; explicit 9-slice (ScaleType=Slice + defined SliceCenter, SliceScale, ScaleType=Tile for textures) strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI stretches a button image (warped corners) or ships fixed-offset square frames that distort/break on resize (the MEAN's fixed-offset square-corner build); a surface system that holds corners and proportion at any size — 9-slice or scale-driven-with-aspect-and-consistent-corners — is the production-grade resize robustness. That commitment is exactly what the GREAT's responsive scale-based layout + UIAspectRatioConstraint + consistent UICorner expresses, and what the MEAN's fixed-offset square frames structurally lack. Grading the scale-aware-resizable-surface commitment keeps this discriminating, with custom-art 9-slice as the full-marks strengthener.

grading.pass: Resizable surfaces are scale-aware — 9-slice (ScaleType=Slice + defined SliceCenter, SliceScale), OR scale-driven sizing with UIAspectRatioConstraint holding proportion and consistent UICorner radius across sizes — so corners stay crisp and proportions undistorted. Explicit 9-slice / Tile textures strengthen it.
grading.partial: Surfaces are scale-driven/rounded in places but proportion-holding (aspect constraint) or corner consistency under resize is only partly committed, OR 9-slice is used on some art while other resizable surfaces still stretch.
grading.fail: Surfaces are fixed-offset square frames (or stretched fixed images) that distort or break on other screen sizes, with no scale-aware surface system.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing a scale-aware resizable-surface system — ImageLabel/ImageButton ScaleType=Slice with a defined SliceCenter (and SliceScale), OR scale-driven sizing with UIAspectRatioConstraint holding proportion and consistent UICorner radius across sizes — so surfaces keep crisp corners/undistorted proportions under resize. Explicit 9-slice (ScaleType=Slice + SliceCenter/SliceScale, ScaleType=Tile for textures) is credited toward full marks. Fixed-offset square-corner frames that break/distort on other screen sizes do NOT satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Make resizable surfaces hold up under scaling: for custom-art panels/buttons set ScaleType=Slice and define SliceCenter as the 3x3 divider (use SliceScale to grow the border, ScaleType=Tile to repeat textures) so corners stay crisp while edges/center stretch; for Frame-based surfaces, size them by Scale, hold proportion with UIAspectRatioConstraint, and keep UICorner radius consistent across sizes — instead of fixed-offset square frames that distort or break on resize.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar gated the pass strictly on ScaleType=Slice/SliceCenter custom-image 9-slice, which the GREAT design-claim never names — so the previous note said both artifacts share the absence and the criterion can't discriminate. The underlying axis is 'do resizable surfaces hold their corners/proportions under scaling, or do they distort/break' — and on that axis the artifacts diverge sharply: the MEAN explicitly ships 'fixed pixel OFFSETS ... square corners ... breaks on other screen sizes' (surfaces that distort/break on resize), while the GREAT explicitly commits to a 'fully responsive scale-based layout (... UIAspectRatioConstraint/UISizeConstraint) that holds on phone, tablet and desktop' plus 'consistent UICorner radius' (surfaces that hold proportion and rounded corners across sizes). Widening the pass to 'a scale-aware resizable-surface system (9-slice OR scale-driven sizing + aspect-held + consistent rounded corners)' lets the GREAT's responsive/constraint/UICorner commitment clear it while the MEAN's fixed-offset square-frame build fails, restoring discrimination; custom-art 9-slice remains the strengthener for full marks. This grades the resize-robustness capability the GREAT genuinely expresses rather than the single 9-slice API.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — INTERACTIVE FEEDBACK & MOTION. Every interactive element acknowledges input through TweenService-driven micro-feedback — a snappy hover state (scale-up and/or UIStroke 0→2-3px and brightness shift) and a quick press scale-down that settles — and state changes are animated, not hard-cut: menus slide/scale in (start off-screen + Visible, tween to position) instead of blinking in. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to TweenService-driven hover/press feedback AND animated open/close: passing requires the build to state (1) hover and press feedback via real TweenService (not ad-hoc loops) on interactive elements, AND (2) animated panel entrance/exit rather than instant Visible toggling. A build of static buttons with no hover/press response and menus that blink into existence (the clearest 'made in 10 minutes' tell) FAILS. A build that commits to tweened hover/press + animated open/close passes; a behind-the-panel blur on modal open strengthens it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Static buttons feel dead/default and menus that blink in are the clearest 'made in 10 minutes' tell; subtle, fast, consistent state feedback is a top reviewer recommendation ('animation makes everything much better') and reads as a finished product. Using real TweenService (not ad-hoc loops) for hover/press and animating every state change — plus a modal-open blur for focus — is the juice players feel even if they can't name it. Grading the tweened-feedback + animated-transition commitment keeps this discriminating against a static, blink-in build.

grading.pass: TweenService drives hover feedback (scale and/or UIStroke thickness + brightness, snappy ~0.2s ease) and a press scale-down-and-settle on interactive elements, PLUS animated panel entrance/exit (off-screen start → tween in) rather than instant Visible toggling. A behind-panel Lighting blur on modal open strengthens it.
grading.partial: Hover/press feedback OR animated open/close is present but not both (e.g. tweened buttons but menus still blink in), OR feedback uses ad-hoc loops rather than real TweenService.
grading.fail: Buttons are static with no hover/press response and menus blink into existence via instant Visible toggling.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing TweenService-driven hover feedback (scale and/or UIStroke thickness + brightness, snappy ~0.2s ease) and a press scale-down-and-settle on interactive elements, PLUS animated panel entrance/exit (off-screen start → tween in, e.g. Back ease overshoot) rather than instant Visible toggling. A behind-panel Lighting blur on modal open is credited. Static buttons and blink-in menus do not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Wire hover via TweenService (scale up and/or UIStroke 0→2-3px + slight brightness, ~0.2s ease) and press as a quick scale-down that settles; animate menu open/close by starting the frame off-screen and tweening into place (Back ease for a springy feel) instead of toggling Visible; add a Lighting blur when a full-screen menu opens.

criteria.statement: Animation has a deliberate, consistent PERSONALITY rather than no animation or one default tween: the build commits to an easing family chosen to match the UI's tone (Sine/Quad Out for calm/premium, Back/Elastic for playful) applied consistently across transitions, and/or staggered list/grid child reveals. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to intentional, tone-matched, consistent easing (and ideally stagger): passing requires the build to state that its transitions use a chosen easing personality tied to the UI's tone, applied consistently — not the absence of animation and not a single undifferentiated default/linear tween. A build with 'no transitions' and no animation FAILS. A build that commits to tweened transitions with a chosen, tone-matched easing personality passes; staggered child reveals strengthen it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI has no animation (the MEAN) or one default tween; choosing an easing curve tied to tone and applying it consistently sets the emotional personality of the whole interface. Grading the tone-matched-easing commitment keeps it discriminating against the MEAN's no-animation build, while a bare 'it has tweens' without tonal intent correctly lands partial.

grading.pass: Tweened transitions use an easing personality chosen to match the UI's tone, applied consistently; staggered child reveals strengthen it.
grading.partial: Tweened transitions are committed but the easing is generic/default or its tone-match isn't stated, OR easing is intentional but inconsistent / lacks stagger.
grading.fail: No animation/transitions, or a single undifferentiated default/linear tween with no tonal intent.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing tweened transitions with an easing personality chosen to match the UI's tone (Sine/Quad Out premium, Back/Elastic playful) applied consistently, and/or staggered list/grid child reveals. Named curve family and stagger strengthen it. 'No transitions' / no animation, or a single undifferentiated default/linear tween, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Pick an easing personality matching the game's tone (Sine/Quad Out for calm/premium, Back/Elastic for playful) and use it consistently for all transitions, and stagger list/grid child reveals for a cascading entrance — instead of shipping no animation or one default linear tween.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar required an explicitly named easing family tied to tone plus staggered reveals; the GREAT design-claim said 'tweened open/close/hover transitions (juice)' but didn't name the curve, so it failed and tied the MEAN's 'no transitions'. The GREAT clearly commits to a deliberate animation system ('juice' = intentional motion personality), while the MEAN explicitly ships zero animation. Re-anchoring pass to 'committed tweened transitions with a chosen tone-matched easing personality' lets the GREAT's juice commitment clear it (a bare 'has tweens' lands partial without the tone-match) while the MEAN's no-animation build fails, restoring discrimination; named curve + stagger remain strengtheners.

criteria.statement: Interactive feedback is wired as a SYSTEM that scales to dynamically-created elements and is input-correct, not just hand-attached to load-time buttons: the build commits to feedback that auto-applies to runtime-spawned elements (a DescendantAdded-driven linker, OR self-contained feedback baked into reusable component templates) AND interaction bound to the cross-platform Activated event (mouse/touch/gamepad) rather than mouse-only clicks. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to scalable, input-correct feedback wiring: passing requires the build to state (1) feedback that applies to runtime-added/template-instantiated elements (auto-wiring or component-carried) AND (2) Activated-based interaction. A build with 'static TextButtons' and 'no hover/press feedback' FAILS. A build that commits to a feedback system covering spawned/templated elements via Activated passes; an explicit DescendantAdded linker with HoverImage/PressedImage strengthens it. NOTE: discrimination for THIS pair is partial — the MEAN explicitly has 'no hover/press feedback' (clean fail), but the GREAT commits to hover/press feedback via reusable templates WITHOUT naming DescendantAdded auto-wiring or Activated, so it may land partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Naive UI only animates load-time buttons (spawned cards are dead) and wires mouse-only clicks; a DescendantAdded-or-component feedback system plus Activated is a scalability+correctness practice the MEAN's static-no-feedback build entirely lacks. Grading the scalable-feedback + Activated commitment keeps the fail-pin sharp against the MEAN; where the GREAT commits template-carried feedback but not Activated, it honestly lands partial.

grading.pass: Feedback auto-applies to runtime-spawned/template-instantiated elements (DescendantAdded linker OR component-carried feedback) AND interaction is bound to Activated, with HoverImage/PressedImage where applicable.
grading.partial: Feedback is committed (hover/press, including via reusable templates) but only one of {covers spawned/templated elements, Activated-bound} is stated, so the system is partly committed.
grading.fail: Static buttons with no hover/press feedback, or feedback only on load-time buttons wired to mouse-only clicks.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing feedback auto-applied to runtime-spawned/template-instantiated elements (a DescendantAdded linker, OR feedback baked into reusable component templates) AND interaction bound to the Activated event (not MouseButton1Click), with HoverImage/PressedImage where applicable. An explicit DescendantAdded linker strengthens it. Feedback only on static load-time buttons, or no feedback at all, does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Build feedback as a system: bake hover/press tweens+sounds into reusable component templates (or link them via a PlayerGui.DescendantAdded listener) so runtime-spawned/templated cards behave identically, and bind interaction to the Activated event (mouse/touch/gamepad correct) — instead of static buttons with no feedback.
criteria.change_reason: Largely a true gap: the GREAT commits to 'polished interactive feedback with hover and press states' carried by 'reusable component templates' but does NOT state DescendantAdded auto-wiring or Activated binding, so it failed the old bar's strict dual requirement alongside the MEAN's no-feedback build. The MEAN explicitly has 'no hover/press feedback'. The rewrite keeps the fail bar pinned to the MEAN's no-feedback default and the pass bar at the system minimum (covers spawned/templated elements + Activated); component-carried feedback (which the GREAT's templates imply) now counts toward the spawned-coverage half, but without an Activated commitment the GREAT honestly lands partial. The sharp edge is the fail-pin to the MEAN's stated absence; the rewrite accepts component-carried feedback (not only DescendantAdded) so the GREAT's template-feedback commitment is credited rather than ignored.

criteria.statement: Text carries IN-CONTENT emphasis through a deliberate type/color system rather than one flat default treatment everywhere: the build commits to differentiating emphasis within text — ideally RichText (RichText=true with inline tags coloring/weighting parts of a single string: damage numbers, highlighted keywords), OR at minimum a committed multi-tier weighted type scale plus the constrained palette's accent applied to emphasize specific text (header/keyword/value standing out from body) — not 'one default font size' and one flat color on every label. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to differentiated, system-driven text emphasis versus one undifferentiated default treatment: passing requires the build to state either RichText inline emphasis, OR a multi-tier size+weight type scale with palette-accent emphasis applied to distinguish important text from body. A build of plain labels at 'one default font size' and default colors (one flat treatment everywhere) FAILS. A build that commits to RichText inline styling passes outright; a committed weighted type scale + accent emphasis passes; RichText with correct escaping and localization-reapply awareness strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic UI uses one default font size and one flat color per label (the MEAN), so nothing in the text stands out; differentiated emphasis — RichText inline styling, or a weighted type scale with an accent applied to key text — is a clear quality step. That differentiation is exactly what the GREAT's 'consistent type scale' + constrained-palette accent expresses, and what the MEAN's single-default-size/flat-color build structurally lacks. Grading the differentiated-text-emphasis commitment keeps this discriminating, with RichText inline styling (and its escaping/localization caveats) as the full-marks path.

grading.pass: Text emphasis is differentiated by a system — RichText inline tags coloring/weighting parts of a single string, OR a committed multi-tier size+weight type scale plus palette-accent emphasis distinguishing key text from body. RichText with escaping + localization-strips-markup awareness strengthens it.
grading.partial: A weighted type scale is committed but in-content/accent emphasis is weak or unstated (size tiers only, no accent or in-string emphasis), so differentiation is only partial.
grading.fail: One default font size and one flat color on every label (or separate labels merely for emphasis), with no RichText and no weighted-scale + accent emphasis.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing differentiated, system-driven text emphasis — RichText (RichText=true with inline tags) coloring/weighting parts of a single string, OR a committed multi-tier size+weight type scale plus palette-accent emphasis distinguishing important text from body. RichText with correct escaping and localization-strips-markup awareness is credited toward full marks. 'One default font size' with default colors / one flat treatment on every label does NOT satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix:
Differentiate text emphasis with a system: enable RichText=true and embed inline tags (, , ,
) to emphasize parts of one string (damage numbers, keywords), escaping literals and re-applying after localization; at minimum, commit to a multi-tier size+weight type scale and apply the palette accent to the text that should stand out — instead of one default font size and one flat color on every label.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar gated the pass strictly on RichText=true inline tags, which the GREAT design-claim never names, and explicitly said a type scale across separate labels 'does not satisfy this' — so the GREAT failed alongside the MEAN's flat-color labels, zero discrimination. The underlying axis is 'is text emphasis differentiated by a system, or one flat default treatment everywhere' — and the artifacts diverge: the MEAN explicitly ships 'one default font size' with default colors (one flat treatment), while the GREAT commits to 'a consistent type scale' (multi-tier size+weight) plus 'a constrained palette' with 'a single accent reserved for the call-to-action' (accent-driven emphasis). Widening the pass to 'differentiated, system-driven text emphasis (RichText inline OR a committed weighted type scale + accent emphasis)' lets the GREAT's type-scale + accent commitment clear it while the MEAN's one-flat-size build fails, restoring discrimination; RichText inline styling remains the outright/strengthening path for full marks. This honestly grades the differentiated-text-emphasis capability the GREAT expresses while keeping the floor pinned to the MEAN's flat default.

criteria.statement: Stateful, scalable UI is built as reusable components instantiated with props and driven by state, rather than duplicated hand-placed instances: the build commits to a component model where one component definition is reused with different props (one Menu/Card reused), visibility/values are state-driven, and structure is declarative — not each screen hand-built instance-by-instance. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a reusable, prop/state-driven component architecture: passing requires the build to state reusable components instantiated with props/state-driven updates (React-Luau-style, or an equivalent reusable-template-with-state model) replacing duplicated hand-placed instances. A build of 'elements hand-placed by absolute position' in a ScreenGui with no reuse FAILS. A build that commits to a reusable prop/state-driven component architecture passes; useState/useEffect-with-deps/useRef and isolated Storybook/UILabs preview strengthen it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Modern Roblox UI is built from components reused across menus with state-driven updates, far beyond hand-placed instances that can't scale or stay consistent (the MEAN). Grading the reusable-prop/state-component commitment (accepting the reusable-template-with-state altitude the GREAT expresses) keeps it discriminating against hand-placed duplication, with the specific hooks/Storybook as strengtheners.

grading.pass: Reusable components are instantiated with props and driven by state (one component reused, state-driven visibility/values, declarative structure). useState/useEffect-with-deps+cleanup/useRef and isolated Storybook/UILabs preview strengthen it.
grading.partial: Reusable templates/components are committed but without a state-driven dimension (props only, no state-driven updates), OR a few components amid mostly hand-placed instances.
grading.fail: Hand-placed, duplicated instances in a ScreenGui with no component reuse or state-driven structure.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing reusable components instantiated with props and driven by state (one component reused with different props; visibility/values state-driven; declarative structure) — React-Luau-style or an equivalent reusable-template-with-state model — replacing duplicated hand-placed instances. useState/useEffect-with-deps+cleanup/useRef and isolated Storybook/UILabs preview strengthen it. Hand-placed duplicated instances with no reuse do not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Build the UI as reusable components: define one component taking props (one Menu/Card reused with different props), drive visibility/values from state, keep structure declarative, and iterate components in isolation (Storybook/UILabs) — instead of hand-placing duplicated instances per screen.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar demanded React-Luau hooks specifically (useState/useEffect/useRef/Storybook) and explicitly rejected 'reusable component templates' — but the GREAT design-claim's 'reusable component templates' IS a component-reuse commitment, expressed at the design altitude, so it failed and tied the MEAN's hand-placed build. Re-anchoring pass to accept 'reusable components instantiated with props + state-driven updates' (including the reusable-template-with-state model the GREAT expresses) lets the GREAT clear it while the MEAN's hand-placed-no-reuse build fails; the specific hooks/Storybook become strengtheners. A bare 'templates' with no state-driven dimension lands partial, keeping sharpness.

criteria.statement: Presentation is SEPARATED from data so the UI is not a pile of static instances with values baked in: the build commits to a layer that decouples what is shown from the data behind it — ideally an external reactive store (e.g. Charm) the UI subscribes to with a view-state-vs-game-state boundary and binding/spring-driven per-frame animation, OR at minimum a reusable component/template layer instantiated/fed FROM data (one template populated per data item) rather than each value hand-placed into a unique static instance. The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a presentation/data separation (data drives reusable templates, ideally via a reactive store) versus a static hand-placed GUI with data conflated into instances: passing requires the build to state that the UI is produced from data through a reusable component/template layer (data-driven instantiation), with the strongest builds adding an external reactive store + view-state boundary + binding-driven animation. A build that is a static hand-placed GUI with no data/template layer (values baked into hand-placed instances) FAILS. A build that commits to a data-fed reusable component/template layer passes; an external reactive store (Charm) with a view-state-vs-game-state boundary and useBinding/spring per-frame animation strengthens it toward full marks.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Conflating data into the UI (values baked into hand-placed static instances, the MEAN) is the coupling that makes generic UI unmaintainable; separating presentation from data — a reusable template layer fed from data, ideally an external reactive store with a view-state boundary and binding-driven animation — is real software architecture. The data-fed-template separation is exactly what the GREAT's 'reusable component templates instead of hand-positioned offsets' expresses, and what the MEAN's static hand-placed GUI structurally lacks. Grading the presentation/data-separation commitment keeps this discriminating, with the external reactive store + bindings as the full-marks strengthener.

grading.pass: Presentation is decoupled from data — a reusable component/template layer instantiated/fed from data (one template per data item); at full strength an external reactive store (Charm) the UI subscribes to, with a view-state-vs-game-state boundary and binding/spring-driven per-frame animation.
grading.partial: A reusable template layer is committed but its data-driven instantiation isn't clearly stated (templates without a data-feed), OR a partial separation exists without a store/view-state boundary, so decoupling is only partly committed.
grading.fail: A static hand-placed GUI with values baked into instances and no data/template layer (game data conflated into the UI), and/or state-driven per-frame animation only.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing presentation decoupled from data — a reusable component/template layer instantiated/fed FROM data (one template populated per data item), ideally an external reactive store (e.g. Charm) the UI subscribes to with a view-state-vs-game-state boundary and binding/spring-driven per-frame animation — rather than a static hand-placed GUI with values baked into instances. The external store + view-state boundary + useBinding/spring animation is credited toward full marks. A static hand-placed GUI with data conflated into instances and no data/template layer does NOT satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Separate presentation from data: render the UI from data through a reusable component/template layer (one template instantiated/populated per data item) instead of hand-placing each value into a unique static instance; for full marks, move game data (coins, inventory, settings) into an external reactive store (Charm) the UI subscribes to — keeping UI-only view state (open menu, selected tab) in the component layer — and drive continuous/per-frame animation through bindings (useBinding) or a spring library rather than state.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar gated the pass strictly on an external reactive store (Charm) + view-state boundary + binding-driven animation, and explicitly said 'reusable component templates ... do not satisfy this' — so the GREAT (which commits to 'reusable component templates' but names no store) failed alongside the MEAN's static no-data-layer build, zero discrimination. The discriminating axis is 'is presentation decoupled from data, or are values baked into static hand-placed instances' — and the artifacts diverge: the MEAN is explicitly 'a static hand-placed GUI ... elements hand-placed by absolute position' (data conflated into instances, no data/template layer), while the GREAT commits to 'reusable component templates instead of hand-positioned offsets' (a presentation layer separable from, and fed by, data). Widening the pass to 'presentation/data separation via a data-fed reusable component/template layer (external reactive store as the full-marks strengthener)' lets the GREAT's component-template commitment clear it while the MEAN's static-baked-in build fails, restoring discrimination. The external store + binding-driven animation remains the strengthener for full marks, so a bare static GUI still fails and the store-architecture sharpness is preserved at the top end — this grades the separation-of-concerns capability the GREAT genuinely expresses rather than only the specific store API.

criteria.statement: Complex screens are COMPOSED as a deliberate header/body/footer information system that steers the eye, not a flat undifferentiated layout: the build commits to a vertical composition (framing header/footer around a distinct body) AND a stated mechanism directing attention to key info (color weight, gradient direction, or a stated focal-flow). The discriminator is whether the build COMMITS to a header/body/footer composition with directed focal flow: passing requires the build to state both a deliberate framing structure (header/body/footer or equivalent zoned composition) and an eye-steering mechanism toward key info. A build of plain Frames/TextLabels 'hand-placed by absolute position' with 'default gray/white colors' and no composition FAILS. A build that commits to a header/body/footer composition with a stated focal-flow mechanism passes; darker-header/footer-framing-lighter-body with gradient direction strengthens it.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Treating UI as an information-navigation system with intentional framing and focal flow is what separates a designed shop/menu from a flat grid; the MEAN is a flat undifferentiated absolute-placed layout with no composition or focal gravity. Grading the framing-composition + focal-flow commitment keeps it discriminating against the MEAN, while a build that states only focal flow (no framing structure) correctly lands partial.

grading.pass: A deliberate header/body/footer (or zoned) composition is committed AND an eye-steering mechanism (color weight and/or gradient direction and/or stated focal-flow) pulls attention to key info. Darker-header/footer-framing-lighter-body with gradient direction strengthens it.
grading.partial: A framing composition OR a directed focal-flow mechanism is committed but not both (e.g. visual hierarchy toward a primary action without a stated header/body/footer framing), so composition is only partly committed.
grading.fail: A flat undifferentiated layout (hand-placed, default colors) with no header/body/footer composition and no focal gravity.

criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing a deliberate header/body/footer (or equivalent zoned) composition AND an eye-steering mechanism (color weight and/or gradient direction and/or a stated focal-flow) pulling attention to key info. Darker header/footer framing a lighter body with gradient direction strengthens it. A flat undifferentiated hand-placed layout with default colors does not satisfy this.
criteria.concrete_fix: Compose complex screens with a deliberate header/body/footer structure (e.g. darker header and footer framing a lighter body) and use color weight and/or gradient direction to pull the eye toward the key info — treating the screen as a navigable information system rather than a flat grid of hand-placed elements.
criteria.change_reason: Old bar required an explicit darker-header/footer + gradient-direction statement; the GREAT design-claim's 'clear visual hierarchy guiding the eye to the primary action' is a directed-focal-flow commitment but it didn't state the header/body/footer framing structure, so it failed and tied the MEAN's flat hand-placed build. Re-anchoring pass to 'committed framing composition AND a stated eye-steering mechanism' lets a build that commits to both clear it, while the MEAN's flat undifferentiated absolute-placed gray layout fails. Where the GREAT states focal flow but not the framing structure, it lands partial — but the fail-pin to the MEAN's flat composition is sharp, restoring discrimination from the previous both-fail tie.
